141981.text: kubeadm: fixed a preflight check on OpenRC systems that reported a service as enabled whenever `rc-update show default` mentioned its name anywhere, including as part of another service's name.
141981.markdown: Kubeadm: fixed a preflight check on OpenRC systems that reported a service as enabled whenever `rc-update show default` mentioned its name anywhere, including as part of another service's name. ([#141981](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141981), [@thc1006](https://github.com/thc1006)) [SIG Cluster Lifecycle]
141981.author: thc1006
141981.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

[`ServiceIsEnabled`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b1856e29a9c992113d5db00096082ddcc3a55d8a/cmd/kubeadm/app/util/initsystem/initsystem_unix.go#L60-L65) searches the whole output of `rc-update show default` for the service name, so another listed service whose name contains it answers for it.

```go
outBytes, _ := exec.Command("rc-update", args...).Output()
return strings.Contains(string(outBytes), service)
```

With `kubelet-debug` or `my-kubelet` in the default runlevel and `kubelet` not added to it, the call returns true for `kubelet`. Preflight [checks that service](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b1856e29a9c992113d5db00096082ddcc3a55d8a/cmd/kubeadm/app/preflight/checks.go#L1160), so the operator never gets the `kubelet service is not enabled, please run 'rc-update add kubelet default'` warning.

A name collision is not the only way to reach that answer. Whether `rc-update` lists a service that is in none of the requested runlevels comes from the environment rather than from its arguments:

```c
verbose = rc_yesno(getenv ("EINFO_VERBOSE"));
```

and that flag is what decides whether the row is printed at all:

```c
if (inone || verbose) {
	printf(" %26s |", service->value);
```

OpenRC exports `EINFO_VERBOSE=yes` when `rc_verbose` is enabled in `/etc/rc.conf`, so a kubeadm run that inherits it gets every known service listed, with the runlevel column blanked for the ones outside default. The substring search then answers true for anything installed.

The call drops the error as well, so if `rc-update` fails partway through, whatever it printed first is still searched.

`rc-update` prints `<service> | <runlevels>` per line, and this compares the two columns instead of the whole listing. It cuts at the last `|` so a service name containing one is not cut short, then looks for `default` among the fields on the right. `rc-update show` always exits 0, so a non-zero status means the command itself failed and there is nothing worth reading.

The parsing lives in `openrcServiceIsEnabled`, which takes the listing as a string, so the test drives it directly rather than putting a fake `rc-update` on `PATH`. The package had no test file. This adds one with twelve cases: the plain enabled service, the two name collisions above, a listing holding more than one service, a service other than `kubelet`, a blanked runlevel column, a different runlevel, a listed name containing the separator, the same name being the one asked about, the wider column, a line with no separator, and an empty listing. The fixtures come from a helper that reproduces the `printf` above rather than hand-counted padding, which I checked by diffing its output against the C. The padding width is not fixed, so the helper prints one width and one case carries a wider one.

Putting each piece of the old behavior back makes named cases fail. `strings.Contains` fails six of the twelve, cutting at the first `|` fails the two separator cases, skipping the runlevel column fails the two runlevel cases, dropping `TrimSpace` fails five, and comparing against a hard-coded `kubelet` rather than the argument fails the two cases that ask about something else.

The three lines that run `rc-update` and drop out on a non-zero status are not covered, since driving them would need the fake binary this test deliberately does not use.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

N/A

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Only `ServiceIsEnabled` changes. `ServiceExists` and `ServiceIsActive` ignore their exit status on purpose, since `rc-service status` reports a stopped or missing service that way and writes it to stderr, which is what the comment above `ServiceExists` is about; #86508 is why `ServiceIsActive` reads the combined output. systemd and Windows are untouched.

A node where `kubelet` really is in the default runlevel keeps getting true. What changes is the node that was getting a false positive and now sees the warning it should have been seeing.

I do not have an OpenRC machine to hand, so the output shapes come from [`show()`](https://github.com/OpenRC/openrc/blob/e877fe9f5d6ce238862516ce84a405a12fd721a2/src/rc-update/rc-update.c#L161-L205) rather than from a capture. The `boot` case is there to pin the column comparison; `show default` itself only ever prints `default` or blanks in that column.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
kubeadm: fixed a preflight check on OpenRC systems that reported a service as enabled whenever `rc-update show default` mentioned its name anywhere, including as part of another service's name.
```

<!--

Optionally add one or more of the following kinds if applicable:
/kind api-change

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
The CEL cost estimator for URL accessor functions (`getScheme`, `getHostname`, `getHost`, `getPort`, `getEscapedPath`, `getQuery`) does not set a `ResultSize` on the returned CallEstimate. This causes any downstream string operation (e.g. `matches()`) on the result to treat it as `unbounded (MaxUint64)`, even when the input URL has a known maxLength.

For example, `url(self).getEscapedPath().matches(regex)` on a field with `maxLength: 300` produces an estimated cost exceeding the per-rule budget by 100x, because `matches()` cannot see the `300-character` bound through `getEscapedPath()`.

This fixes the issue by setting ResultSize to the target URL's size estimate for most accessors, and to 3x the target's size for `getEscapedPath` since percent-encoding can expand each byte into 3 characters (`%XX`). This is consistent with how `substring()` and `trim()` already propagate `ResultSize`. Overflow-safe multiplication via `SizeEstimate.Multiply()` is used for the 3x factor.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Related:  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140205 discovered post this
<!--

Do not use "Fixes" if the PR is of kind `failing-test` or `flake`.

KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/<kep-issue-number>

If there is no associated issue, then write "N/A".
-->

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

This is a cost estimate decrease. CRDs that were previously rejected due to URL accessor results being treated as unbounded will now be accepted. The change only affects compile-time cost estimation, not runtime behavior. The URL accessor cost `(Min: 1, Max: 1)` is unchanged. Only ResultSize is added. For `getScheme`, `getHostname`, `getHost`, `getPort`, and `getQuery`, the bound equals the target URL's size since these return substrings. For `getEscapedPath`, the bound is 3x the target's size to account for worst-case percent-encoding. Unit tests verify ResultSize propagation for each accessor, and cost stability tests verify that `url(self.val1).getXxx().matches()` on a bounded field produces finite, reasonable costs.

142003.text: Fixed DRA kubelet plugin helper rolling updates for drivers with long valid names by shortening automatic DRA service socket paths when needed.
142003.markdown: Fixed DRA kubelet plugin helper rolling updates for drivers with long valid names by shortening automatic DRA service socket paths when needed. ([#142003](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142003), [@ryo-whaletech](https://github.com/ryo-whaletech)) [SIG Node]
142003.author: ryo-whaletech
142003.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig node
/wg device-management

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

With `RollingUpdate`, the DRA kubelet plugin helper normally uses `dra-<Pod UID>.sock` for the automatic service socket. The default plugin directory also contains the full driver name, so a valid 37-byte driver name makes the full endpoint exactly 108 bytes and therefore unusable as a pathname-based AF_UNIX socket.

This change preserves `dra-<Pod UID>.sock` whenever the full path fits. If it would exceed the AF_UNIX limit, the helper switches to a deterministic shortened basename containing 64 bits of the Pod UID's SHA-256 digest encoded with URL-safe, unpadded Base64. With the default directory and the maximum valid 63-byte driver name, the resulting endpoint is 104 bytes.

Non-rolling `dra.sock` naming, ordinary short-driver rolling naming, and explicit `PluginSocket` behavior remain unchanged. Arbitrary custom `PluginDataDirectoryPath` values are not guaranteed to fit.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142002

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Related work is distinct: #139166 and #139623 addressed the rolling registration socket under `plugins_registry`; #139623 explicitly left `dra-<uid>.sock` service sockets unchanged. #141815 corrected the registration fallback's exact-108 boundary. #140837 added kubelet-side endpoint and driver validation, but does not prevent this helper from generating an invalid automatic service endpoint.

Verification on Kubernetes master `3af569e862d19a046cdfd63cda837f9bb29da6fa` with Go 1.27.1:

142013.text: resource.Quantity.Cmp and CmpInt64 now return the correct result when the two quantities' scales differ by more than an int32 can represent.
142013.markdown: Resource.Quantity.Cmp and CmpInt64 now return the correct result when the two quantities' scales differ by more than an int32 can represent. ([#142013](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142013), [@thc1006](https://github.com/thc1006)) [SIG API Machinery]
142013.author: thc1006
142013.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig api-machinery

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`Quantity.Cmp` can panic, or take a very long time, when the two values it compares have scales that are far apart.

`int64Amount.Cmp` subtracts the two scales as an `int32`, and that difference does not have to fit in an `int32`. `1e2147483647` parses to `int64Amount{value: 1, scale: 2147483647}`, so comparing it against a nanoscale value subtracts `2147483647 - (-9)`, which wraps to a negative number. `divideByScaleInt64` passes that to `pow10Int64`, gets back `0`, and divides by it. A little below the point where it wraps, the comparison falls through to `inf.Dec` instead, which lines the two values up by writing the whole scale gap out in digits. The scale comes straight from the parsed text, so neither path is bounded by how large the numbers actually are.

The fix does the subtraction in `int64`. When the `int64` fast path cannot represent the result, it settles the comparison from the range of the decimal exponents before reaching `inf.Dec`: a number with `n` bits has between `n/4` and `n/3 + 1` decimal digits, which is enough to bracket the two exponents without counting them. `Quantity.Cmp` and `Quantity.CmpInt64` go through the same helper on their decimal path.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Part of #141166.

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

I checked the result against `big.Rat` over a grid of int64- and decimal-backed operands; every pair that `inf.Dec` can already compare gets the same answer. The added test pins the pairs the old code could not handle, the ones that wrapped onto a zero divisor and the ones that aligned on the exponent.

The exponent-bounds helper is the one from #141348. Once this lands, the ratio path there can drop its own comparator and use `Cmp`.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
resource.Quantity.Cmp and CmpInt64 now return the correct result when the two quantities' scales differ by more than an int32 can represent.
```

142035.text:
kube-proxy no longer tries to set the `nf_conntrack_max` sysctl if its
value is already higher than the value kube-proxy wants it to be. This
fixes a regression in 1.36 on systems where kube-proxy does not have
permission to modify the sysctls, since the new maximum value for
`nf_conntrack_max` could cause kube-proxy to now want a different
(lower) value than it had before.
142035.markdown:
Kube-proxy no longer tries to set the `nf_conntrack_max` sysctl if its
  value is already higher than the value kube-proxy wants it to be. This
  fixes a regression in 1.36 on systems where kube-proxy does not have
  permission to modify the sysctls, since the new maximum value for
  `nf_conntrack_max` could cause kube-proxy to now want a different
  (lower) value than it had before. ([#142035](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142035), [@danwinship](https://github.com/danwinship)) [SIG Network]
142035.author: danwinship
142035.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug
/kind regression

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
#137002 (in 1.36) changed kube-proxy to cap the value of `nf_conntrack_max` (and the associated `hashsize` parameter) so that it didn't grow ridiculously large on machines with lots of cores.

But this means that if someone was previously manually setting `nf_conntrack_max` to the correct value and then running kube-proxy without the ability to modify that sysctl, that kube-proxy would now fail, because "the correct value" is now different.

Years ago, #103174 tried to fix a similar problem by making kube-proxy's behavior be "only change a sysctl if its current value is lower than the value we want", but this was later reverted (#120448) because that behavior doesn't make sense for sysctls in general. This PR brings back that behavior for just `nf_conntrack_max`.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Fixes #141943

#### Special notes for your reviewer:
I had another version of this that _just_ fixed the bug without the unit test changes, etc, which is maybe more backport-able, but I didn't like the fact that it was untested...

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
kube-proxy no longer tries to set the `nf_conntrack_max` sysctl if its
```

#### What type of PR is this?

<!--
Add one of the following kinds:
/kind bug

/kind documentation
/kind feature

Optionally add one or more of the following kinds if applicable:
/kind api-change
/kind deprecation
/kind failing-test
/kind flake
/kind regression
-->
/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
A project that needs a string rule the built-in formats do not cover has to write `+k8s:customValidation` and a function per use, or fork the generator.

This adds `--validation-extensions-file`, a YAML file the **stock** `validation-gen` binary reads at generation time:

```yaml
formats:
  - name: example-uri
    docs: This field holds an absolute URI, with a scheme.
    pattern: '^[a-z][a-z0-9+.-]*://[^\s]+$'
    message: must be an absolute URI with a scheme
```

```
validation-gen --validation-extensions-file=path/to/extensions.yaml ...
```

`+k8s:format=example-uri` then works wherever a built-in format does, composing with `eachVal`, `eachKey`, `ifMode` and `ifEnabled`, and carrying a `format=example-uri` origin. Each pattern compiles to one package-level variable, however many fields use it, and `--docs` lists the project's formats alongside the built-in ones.

Files are checked once, before generation, so a mistake names its source rather than surfacing at the first use of the tag. A project may not redefine a built-in format or take the reserved `k8s-` prefix, so a tag means the same thing in every project that has it. The flag may be repeated and a file may hold several YAML documents; formats concatenate across both, and a name may only be declared once across all of them.

A pattern is the only backing a format has here. A shared Go function, a CEL expression and length bounds fit as keys beside `pattern`; `formats` is one key at the top level so named validations can be added as a sibling section.

142118.text: Out-of-tree kube-scheduler plugins using the `NominatedPodsForNode` method must now pass `logger klog.Logger` as the first argument.
142118.markdown: Out-of-tree kube-scheduler plugins using the `NominatedPodsForNode` method must now pass `logger klog.Logger` as the first argument. ([#142118](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142118), [@jdzikowski](https://github.com/jdzikowski)) [SIG Scheduling and Testing]
142118.author: jdzikowski
142118.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind cleanup
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Propagates contextual `logger klog.Logger` to `PodNominator.NominatedPodsForNode` and `ctx context.Context`  to `SchedulingQueue.GetPod`.

This allows queue and nomination lookup operations to forward contextual loggers to internal helpers and error handlers (`utilruntime.HandleErrorWithLogger`). This solves the TODO we had in [`workload_forest.go`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/83619fca3eed26f9f7cba894d74c00ddb79dfded/pkg/scheduler/backend/queue/workload_forest.go#L136-L137)
#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
N/A
#### Special notes for your reviewer:
1. **`SchedulingQueue.GetPod(ctx context.Context, ...)`**: Updated to accept `context.Context` instead of `klog.Logger`. Since `GetPod` is primarily called from unit and integration tests where `ctx` is already present, passing `ctx` directly avoids wrapping every call with `klog.FromContext(ctx)` and keeps future `ctx` propagation open without tripping `logcheck`. Internally, `GetPod` extracts the logger via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` to call the private `getPod` helper.
2. **`PodNominator.NominatedPodsForNode(logger klog.Logger, ...)`**: Kept `klog.Logger` here so the entire `PodNominator` interface remains consistent (`AddNominatedPod`, `DeleteNominatedPodIfExists`, `UpdateNominatedPod`, and `NominatedPodsForNode` all take `logger klog.Logger`).
#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Action required: Out-of-tree kube-scheduler plugins using the `NominatedPodsForNode` method must now pass `logger klog.Logger` as the first argument.
```

```docs
```

142131.text: Fixed false fractional-byte warnings for integer resource quantities larger than the int64 range.
142131.markdown: Fixed false fractional-byte warnings for integer resource quantities larger than the int64 range. ([#142131](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142131), [@6democratickim9](https://github.com/6democratickim9)) [SIG API Machinery]
142131.author: 6democratickim9
142131.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig api-machinery

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The Pod and PersistentVolumeClaim warning paths detect fractional byte quantities by calling `MilliValue()` and checking the remainder modulo 1000. `MilliValue()` saturates when a quantity exceeds the int64 range, so a whole-byte quantity such as `9223372036854775808` is projected to `MaxInt64` and incorrectly reported as fractional.

This PR checks whether converting the original quantity to scale zero is exact. That determines whether the quantity contains a fractional byte without projecting it through int64.

Regression tests cover Pod container requests and limits, Pod overhead, and PersistentVolumeClaim storage requests and limits. The existing fractional-value tests continue to verify that actual fractional bytes produce warnings.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Part of #141166

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Verified with:

```
go test ./pkg/api/pod ./pkg/api/persistentvolumeclaim -count=1
```

```release-note
Fixed false fractional-byte warnings for integer resource quantities larger than the int64 range.
```

142154.text: Fixed an issue where HorizontalPodAutoscaler incorrectly included pod overhead in the request calculation for pods using pod-level resources.
142154.markdown: Fixed an issue where HorizontalPodAutoscaler incorrectly included pod overhead in the request calculation for pods using pod-level resources. ([#142154](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142154), [@sophieliu15](https://github.com/sophieliu15)) [SIG Apps and Autoscaling]
142154.author: sophieliu15
142154.pr_body:
When evaluating pod-level resource requests in `calculatePodLevelRequests`, `ReplicaCalculator` previously passed an uninitialized `PodResourcesOptions`, defaulting `ExcludeOverhead` to `false`. This included `pod.spec.overhead` in the request denominator, depressing calculated utilization for sandboxed workloads and breaking parity with container-level calculations that do not include overhead.

This change sets `ExcludeOverhead` to `true` so that pod-level and container-level request evaluations remain consistent with container cgroup metrics.

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig autoscaling
/area hpa

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
When evaluating pod-level resource requests in `calculatePodLevelRequests`, `ReplicaCalculator` previously passed an uninitialized `resourcehelpers.PodResourcesOptions{}`, which defaults `ExcludeOverhead` to `false`. As a result, `resourcehelpers.PodRequests` included `pod.spec.overhead` in the request calculation.
This causes two issues in HPA:
1. **Metric Boundary Mismatch:** HPA calculates utilization as `∑ Usage(p) / ∑ Request(p)`. The usage metrics scraped by metrics-server/Kubelet (`/metrics/resource`) measure container cgroups only (`cri-containerd-<CID>.scope`). Sandbox runtime overhead (e.g. Kata Containers, gVisor) runs outside container cgroups in the pod sandbox slice and is not included in container usage metrics. Adding overhead to the request denominator artificially lowers calculated utilization and delays scale-up.
2. **Asymmetry with Container Requests:** When pod-level resources are not specified, `calculatePodRequestsFromContainers` sums container requests and never includes `pod.spec.overhead`. Workloads configured with pod-level resources should evaluate compute utilization identically to workloads configured with container requests.
This change sets `ExcludeOverhead: true` in `calculatePodLevelRequests`, ensuring consistent request baseline evaluation between container-level and pod-level specifications.

142170.text: LimitRanger no longer rejects an update of a PersistentVolumeClaim because of a request that the update leaves unchanged, even when that request is outside the LimitRange minimum or maximum. A changed, added or removed request is checked against both the minimum and the maximum, as on create, so a stored request outside the range is rejected as soon as an update changes it.
142170.markdown: LimitRanger no longer rejects an update of a PersistentVolumeClaim because of a request that the update leaves unchanged, even when that request is outside the LimitRange minimum or maximum. A changed, added or removed request is checked against both the minimum and the maximum, as on create, so a stored request outside the range is rejected as soon as an update changes it. ([#142170](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142170), [@thc1006](https://github.com/thc1006)) [SIG API Machinery and Storage]
142170.author: thc1006
142170.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

LimitRanger checks a PersistentVolumeClaim against the min and max of the LimitRange on create and on every update, and it has only ever looked at the new object (#30145). A request that was accepted when the claim was stored, or that a LimitRange created later no longer allows, fails every update of that claim, even one that only touches labels. #141348 made the comparison exact, which added the requests that used to pass only because both sides were rounded to whole units. For a bound claim the request cannot go down to `status.capacity` or below, so when the max is at or under the capacity nothing satisfies both.

This passes the stored object into `ValidateLimit` and skips the min and max checks for a request that the update leaves as stored. A request that is changed, added or removed is still checked, and so is every other resource in the range and every create. Both objects must have the request and `Cmp` must report the values equal for it to count as unchanged, so `20Gi` and `20480Mi` are one value. It is the ratcheting rule from #141166, and the reasoning #62673 applied to pod updates in 2018.

The test goes through `Validate` with real admission attributes, old and new object included, and each error case checks the exact message, so it also shows which constraint fired. The cases are the rows of the ratcheting table: create, unchanged, changed, added and removed, each on both sides of the range where that applies. With the skip taken out, five cases fail: the four that keep a stored request outside the range, and the one that adds a second resource next to an unchanged one.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Part of #141166

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

This only covers PVCs. Pod updates through the `resize` subresource are in #142171, and `ValidateResourceQuotaUpdate` still checks every entry of `spec.hard`. An apiserver without this change keeps rejecting such an update, so a skewed rollout is no worse than master. `LimitRangerActions` is only implemented by `DefaultLimitRangerActions` in the tree. The LimitRange page on kubernetes.io says an update that violates a constraint is rejected, so I'll send a docs change once this settles.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
LimitRanger no longer rejects an update of a PersistentVolumeClaim because of a request that the update leaves unchanged, even when that request is outside the LimitRange minimum or maximum. A changed, added or removed request is checked against both the minimum and the maximum, as on create, so a stored request outside the range is rejected as soon as an update changes it.
```

142171.text: LimitRanger no longer re-validates the resource requests and limits a pod resize leaves unchanged. Only the values a resize changes are checked against the LimitRange, so an existing pod is no longer rejected on resize by a constraint it already violates.
142171.markdown: LimitRanger no longer re-validates the resource requests and limits a pod resize leaves unchanged. Only the values a resize changes are checked against the LimitRange, so an existing pod is no longer rejected on resize by a constraint it already violates. ([#142171](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142171), [@semx](https://github.com/semx)) [SIG API Machinery and Node]
142171.author: semx
142171.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

On a resize, LimitRanger runs `PodValidateLimitFunc` against the whole pod again: every container, every init container, and the pod-level totals. None of that is scoped to what the resize changed, so a stored value that no longer satisfies a constraint gets rejected on an update that did not touch it. Init containers are included: on master any of them can be resized (`InPlacePodVerticalScalingInitContainers` has defaulted on since v1.36 and is GA and locked on since v1.37), so they are just more containers a resize may or may not have touched.

This follows the ratcheting rule from #141166: a value the stored object already holds is valid by definition. The stored pod is now passed into `PodValidateLimitFunc`, and a check is skipped when the value is unchanged:

- Container level: for a container resource, when both the request and the limit match the container of the same name in the stored pod. Both fields are compared because each of the min, max and ratio constraints reads both the request and the limit. Init containers go through the same check as regular containers.
- Pod level: for a resource, when the pod requests and limits totals match the stored pod's, computed with the same options. This is deliberately about the totals: the pod-type constraint applies to the total, and an unchanged total is the stored one, even when two containers moved in opposite directions. Each of those containers is still checked at the container level.

Anything the resize changes is checked exactly as on create, and create is unchanged (no stored pod, nothing is skipped). The two identical per-container loops are folded into one helper so the skip is applied in one place.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Part of #141166 (LimitRanger line, pod resize side). #142170 added the `oldObj` plumbing and covers the PVC side; this wires the pod branch of `ValidateLimit` that it left unchanged.

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

`TestLimitRangerValidatePodResize` goes through the real `Validate` with the old and new pod on the `resize` subresource, 19 cases: an unchanged container above the max and a resized one above it; an unchanged init container below the min and a resized restartable init container above the max; a cpu resize that leaves the same container's unchanged memory alone; a resize that lowers only the request below the min; an unchanged second container next to a resized one; unchanged and changed pod totals against min and max, and the same for pod-level resources with `PodLevelResources` on; unchanged and changed limit-to-request ratios at the container level and at the pod level; offsetting resizes that leave the pod total unchanged; a resize that adds a limit the stored container did not have (checked, since presence changed); and create being checked in full.

Mutation (`PodMutateLimitFunc`) is not touched; defaulting on resize is unchanged.

Dropped the note on `podRequests` saying init containers cannot be resized: they can on master (the gate is GA since v1.37), the helper reads spec resources regardless, as its function comment already says, and `PodResizeStatus` is deprecated.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
LimitRanger no longer re-validates the resource requests and limits a pod resize leaves unchanged. Only the values a resize changes are checked against the LimitRange, so an existing pod is no longer rejected on resize by a constraint it already violates.
```

142190.text: ResourceQuota updates no longer fail validation on a `spec.hard`, `status.hard` or `status.used` value that the object already holds, so a quota holding a value an older release accepted can still be updated and its status still synced.
142190.markdown: ResourceQuota updates no longer fail validation on a `spec.hard`, `status.hard` or `status.used` value that the object already holds, so a quota holding a value an older release accepted can still be updated and its status still synced. ([#142190](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142190), [@thc1006](https://github.com/thc1006)) [SIG API Machinery and Apps]
142190.author: thc1006
142190.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`ValidateResourceQuotaUpdate` checks the whole new `spec.hard`, and the status update checks every `status.hard` and `status.used` value, without looking at the stored object. The integer check for those values became stricter in c09332890d6. A value past the milli range that the wrapped milli projection used to accept is rejected now, so a quota that stores one cannot be updated at all, not even to change a label. A v1.31 apiserver accepted `spec.hard[pods]: 18446744073709551616m`, because the milli projection wrapped to 0, and the test added with that commit records the lock-out as current behavior.

This compares each value with the one the object already stores under the same key and skips the value checks when the two are equal. Equal means `Quantity.Cmp` returns 0, the comparison the semantic equality for quantities uses. Names are still checked for every entry, scopes and the scope selector as before, and a create is checked in full. A value the update adds or changes is checked as on create. `spec.hard` is compared with the stored `spec.hard`, `status.used` with the stored `status.used`, and `status.hard` with the stored `status.hard` or the stored `spec.hard`. The quota controller writes `spec.hard` into `status.hard` whenever the two differ, and admission enforces `status.hard`. A status the controller cannot write would leave the quota with an empty or stale limit. Only the integer check has changed over time, and a negative value could not have been stored, so nothing new gets in this way.

The test that pinned the lock-out now pins this behavior, with the fractional fixture from that commit and the update and status cases around it.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Related to #141166 (validation compatibility row, ResourceQuota part)

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

An older apiserver in a mixed-version control plane rejects the same update, as it does today. ResourceQuota has no declarative validation tags, so there is no second copy of these rules to keep in step.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
ResourceQuota updates no longer fail validation on a `spec.hard`, `status.hard` or `status.used` value that the object already holds, so a quota holding a value an older release accepted can still be updated and its status still synced.
```

142192.text: Fixed the HorizontalPodAutoscaler utilization and usage calculations wrapping to a wrong or negative current value when pod metric or request totals exceeded int64 or the utilization percentage exceeded int32; the reported percentage now saturates at the int32 limit.
142192.markdown: Fixed the HorizontalPodAutoscaler utilization and usage calculations wrapping to a wrong or negative current value when pod metric or request totals exceeded int64 or the utilization percentage exceeded int32; the reported percentage now saturates at the int32 limit. ([#142192](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142192), [@KR-Ravindra](https://github.com/KR-Ravindra)) [SIG Apps and Autoscaling]
142192.author: KR-Ravindra
142192.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig autoscaling

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`GetResourceUtilizationRatio` sums per-pod metric values and requests as raw `int64`, multiplies the metrics total by 100 and narrows to `int32`. All three steps wrap silently. Near `math.MaxInt64` the HPA ends up with a `currentUtilization` of 0 and a negative raw average, and scales the wrong way or not at all.

The two totals are now accumulated exactly with `math/big`, the percentage is taken exactly, and only the final `int32` narrowing is clamped to `math.MaxInt32`/`math.MinInt32`, so an oversized utilization keeps its direction instead of wrapping. The raw average of `int64` values always fits an `int64`, so `rawAverageValue` is unchanged in type and meaning. `GetMetricUsageRatio` had the same unchecked sum and now accumulates the same way. Nothing changes for inputs that fit today and there is no new error path.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Related to #141166 (HPA row of the Quantity int64 overflow burndown; does not close the tracker)

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Continues #141978, which GitHub closed on a force-push and refuses to reopen; the two review comments from @jpbetz there (doc comment, and the exact sum in `GetMetricUsageRatio`) are addressed in this head. /cc @jpbetz

The `int32` narrowing saturates rather than returning an error, matching the direction-preserving cap taken for replica counts in #141397. If you would rather the HPA surface an error condition when the percentage does not fit, that is a two-line change and I am happy to make it.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed the HorizontalPodAutoscaler utilization and usage calculations wrapping to a wrong or negative current value when pod metric or request totals exceeded int64 or the utilization percentage exceeded int32; the reported percentage now saturates at the int32 limit.
```

142202.text: DRA consumable capacity: requesting capacity had to be done with the capacity name exactly as published by drivers, i.e. typically without the driver name prefix. When requesting with a fully-qualified name, the request failed. Now both unqualified and fully-qualified names work. A related, less likely problem existed when a DRA driver changed how it published capacity and some capacity was allocated already.
142202.markdown: DRA consumable capacity: requesting capacity had to be done with the capacity name exactly as published by drivers, i.e. typically without the driver name prefix. When requesting with a fully-qualified name, the request failed. Now both unqualified and fully-qualified names work. A related, less likely problem existed when a DRA driver changed how it published capacity and some capacity was allocated already. ([#142202](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142202), [@pohly](https://github.com/pohly)) [SIG API Machinery, Apps, Node and Scheduling]
142202.author: pohly
142202.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When the ResourceClaim requested "driver.example.com/bandwidth" and that DRA driver published the capacity as "bandwidth", the request failed. Same for the inverse case.

A less likely problem existed when a DRA driver flipped between publishing with and without its own driver name as prefix: the allocation result stored literally what came from the driver at the time of allocation, which then wouldn't be considered after flipping to the other format.

Nothing prevents DRA drivers and users from publishing resp. requesting the same capacity with and without driver name prefix. Validation could prevent this for ResourceSlices (driver name is known) but doesn't. It's probably also not worth doing because DRA drivers are trusted and  can trivially avoid this; validation would just add overhead. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142218 makes sure that DRA driver behave well.

Lookup for constraints resolves this conflict via "fully-qualified wins". Consumable capacity and CEL resolution was random (last one in map iteration wins), now also prefers fully-qualified.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/140650

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The fix is to normalize names (drop redundant prefix) before comparing. To support downgrades, the allocation result is written with the simpler name without the driver name as prefix because that is what was written in practice before.

I have included making the consumable capacities and CEL capacities/attributes lookup deterministic in this PR. The one about CEL could also be a separate PR, but it seems related enough to not add that review overhead.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
DRA consumable capacity: requesting capacity had to be done with the capacity name exactly as published by drivers, i.e. typically without the driver name prefix. When requesting with a fully-qualified name, the request failed. Now both unqualified and fully-qualified names work. A related, less likely problem existed when a DRA driver changed how it published capacity and some capacity was allocated already.
```

YES: test cases were written manually, then AI was used to fix the code based on a description what the solution should look like.

142214.text: Fixed kubectl describe service printing "+ 0 more..." after the endpoint list when exactly three ready endpoints are followed by not-ready endpoints.
142214.markdown: Fixed kubectl describe service printing "+ 0 more..." after the endpoint list when exactly three ready endpoints are followed by not-ready endpoints. ([#142214](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142214), [@reckless-sherixx](https://github.com/reckless-sherixx)) [SIG CLI]
142214.author: reckless-sherixx
142214.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`formatEndpointSlices` decided that the endpoint list was truncated as soon as it visited a fourth endpoint, but it made that decision before applying the readiness filter while only counting ready endpoints. With exactly three ready endpoints followed by a not-ready one, the not-ready endpoint set the flag without being counted and `kubectl describe service` printed:

```
Endpoints:  10.0.0.1:80,10.0.0.2:80,10.0.0.3:80 + 0 more...
```

This derives the `+ N more...` suffix from the number of ready endpoints after filtering, so the count and the truncation decision always agree. Both the ported and the headless (no ports) branch are fixed.

`TestFormatEndpointSlices` is new; its "three ready endpoints followed by a not ready endpoint" and headless cases fail before the change and pass after it. Also verified failing against the `v1.37.0` tag.

Fixes #142209

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The readiness filter was added in #126932; the `len(list) == max` check predates it and was correct as long as every visited endpoint was counted.

142215.markdown: Kubectl describe node: per-pod resource percentages no longer print -9223372036854775808% on nodes that have not reported allocatable resources, and the "Allocated resources" totals now use the same resource accounting as the per-pod rows. ([#142215](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142215), [@reckless-sherixx](https://github.com/reckless-sherixx)) [SIG CLI]
142215.author: reckless-sherixx
142215.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Two fixes to the per-pod rows of the "Non-terminated Pods" table in `kubectl describe node`:

1. The per-pod percentages divided by the node's allocatable CPU/memory with no zero guard. On a node without `status.allocatable` / `status.capacity` every row printed `100m (-9223372036854775808%)`. The "Allocated resources" totals right below already guard the same division and print `0%`; the rows now do the same via a small `percentOf` helper.

2. Since 97f00d18eeb the rows are computed with `UseStatusResources: true`, but `getPodsTotalRequestsAndLimits` still used the pod spec only, so during an in-place resize a row could show `500m (50%)` while the totals showed `100m (10%)` for the same pod. The totals now use the same `PodResourcesOptions` as the rows.

Two new tests, `TestDescribeNodeResourceWithoutAllocatable` and `TestDescribeNodeResourceUsesStatusResourcesForTotals`, fail before the change and pass after it. Also verified failing against the `v1.37.0` tag.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142210

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Using status resources for the totals follows the scheduler, which accounts allocated (status) resources when they are present. If reviewers would rather have both rows and totals use the spec only, the one-line option change in `getPodsTotalRequestsAndLimits` can be replaced by dropping `UseStatusResources` from the rows instead; the important part is that both agree.

```release-note
kubectl describe node: per-pod resource percentages no longer print -9223372036854775808% on nodes that have not reported allocatable resources, and the "Allocated resources" totals now use the same resource accounting as the per-pod rows.
```

142247.text: Fixed an issue where a Job recreated with the same name as a recently deleted Job could remain unreconciled because it inherited pending Pod expectations from the previous Job.
142247.markdown: Fixed an issue where a Job recreated with the same name as a recently deleted Job could remain unreconciled because it inherited pending Pod expectations from the previous Job. ([#142247](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142247), [@6democratickim9](https://github.com/6democratickim9)) [SIG Apps and Testing]
142247.author: 6democratickim9
142247.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The Job controller tracks pending Pod creations and deletions by namespace/name. If a Job is deleted while a Pod creation is in flight and another Job is immediately created with the same name, the replacement can inherit the old Job's unsatisfied expectation. `syncJob` then skips `manageJob`, leaving the replacement unreconciled until another event or the expectations timeout.

This change clears Pod expectations from the Job delete-event handler, matching the existing behavior of the ReplicaSet and DaemonSet controllers.

It also adds a deterministic integration test. The test blocks the old Job's Pod POST after the creation expectation has been raised, deletes and recreates the Job under the same name with a new UID, waits for the informer to observe the replacement, and then releases the old request. It verifies that the replacement Job is reconciled and receives its suspended condition.

Without the fix, the test reproduces the stale-UID status error from the issue and times out waiting for the replacement Job:

```
Precondition failed: UID in precondition: <old UID>, UID in object meta: <new UID>
```

With the fix, the integration test passes.

I was assigned to #142142 on September 16 and started investigating the reproduction and integration coverage before #142236 was opened. #142236 implements the same expectation cleanup with unit coverage; this PR includes the integration reproduction requested in the issue discussion.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142142

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Local verification:

- The new integration test fails on unmodified `master` with the stale-UID error and an unreconciled replacement Job.
- The new integration test passes three consecutive runs with this change.
- `go test ./pkg/controller/job/...` passes.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed an issue where a Job recreated with the same name as a recently deleted Job could remain unreconciled because it inherited pending Pod expectations from the previous Job.
```


AI assistance was used while investigating the controller flow and developing the integration test. I reviewed the changes and locally verified both the baseline failure and the fixed behavior using a real kube-apiserver and etcd.

142277.text: resource.Quantity: calling String or encoding a quantity is now guaranteed to not mutate the instance. Previously it did in some cases. If you know that an instance will need the string representation multiple times, use CacheString to pre-populate the value at a time when the caller owns the instance and can safely mutate it. This is not necessary for instances coming from ParseQuantity, only for instances created differently or modified through math operations.
142277.markdown: Resource.Quantity: calling String or encoding a quantity is now guaranteed to not mutate the instance. Previously it did in some cases. If you know that an instance will need the string representation multiple times, use CacheString to pre-populate the value at a time when the caller owns the instance and can safely mutate it. This is not necessary for instances coming from ParseQuantity, only for instances created differently or modified through math operations. ([#142277](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142277), [@pohly](https://github.com/pohly)) [SIG API Machinery]
142277.author: pohly
142277.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature
/kind failing-test
/kind flake

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Most of the time, String for a resource.Quantity as returned by ParseQuantity is safe to use concurrently, but not always: when the input string isn't already in the canonical form, then the instance has no cached string and String mutates it when first called, leading to data races. This also happens when encoding as protobuf because Size (another conceptually read-only method) mutates the instance when calling String. Encoding as JSON or CBOR don't do this.

Because it is not predictable for callers when String or encoding are safe when done concurrently, it is better to make both read-only, which matches the normal expectation.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141404

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

To mitigate potential performance regressions during decode + encode, ParseQuantity now always caches a string on all return paths. OTOH, this itself can cause a performance regression when the generated cached string isn't used. The expectation is that non-canonical input is the exception, so hopefully this won't matter.

/assign @jpbetz 

Loosely related to making Quantity safer to use (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141166).

Brought up before in https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0EG7JC6T/p1784208713996489, with no responses. As discussed there and in the issue, data races caused by this have been observed in the kubelet and kube-apiserver.

Mutation was added originally in:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1ef19062096c4fcf8ddeaf3a46731d9f262a0c04/pkg/api/resource/quantity.go#L560-L563

Then converted to string in:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/26033

This is from 2016. In both cases it is unclear which specific use cases benefit from this optimization, so it's a bit hard to tell how relevant this is nowadays. Maybe caching of object serialization (added in 2019, see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/81914) makes it less important?

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
resource.Quantity: calling String or encoding a quantity is now guaranteed to not mutate the instance. Previously it did in some cases. If you know that an instance will need the string representation multiple times, use CacheString to pre-populate the value at a time when the caller owns the instance and can safely mutate it. This is not necessary for instances coming from ParseQuantity, only for instances created differently or modified through math operations.
```

YES: code was generated based on my guidance.

142340.text: Kubelet now reports allocated resource health statuses in deterministic order, preventing unnecessary Pod status updates when resource health is unchanged.
142340.markdown: Kubelet now reports allocated resource health statuses in deterministic order, preventing unnecessary Pod status updates when resource health is unchanged. ([#142340](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142340), [@photoszzt](https://github.com/photoszzt)) [SIG API Machinery, Apps, Auth, Cloud Provider, Node, Release, Scheduling, Storage and Testing]
142340.author: photoszzt
142340.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Canonicalizes `AllocatedResourcesStatus` by resource name and each resource health list by resource ID in both the device manager and DRA manager. This prevents unchanged resource health from producing different serialized Pod statuses and unnecessary API updates.

142350.text: `SelfSignedCertKeyOptions` in `k8s.io/client-go/util/cert` accepts a `KeyGenerator`, allowing self-signed certificates to be generated with a key algorithm other than RSA. The default remains a 2048-bit RSA key.
142350.markdown: `SelfSignedCertKeyOptions` in `k8s.io/client-go/util/cert` accepts a `KeyGenerator`, allowing self-signed certificates to be generated with a key algorithm other than RSA. The default remains a 2048-bit RSA key. ([#142350](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142350), [@antcybersec](https://github.com/antcybersec)) [SIG API Machinery and Auth]
142350.author: antcybersec
142350.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`GenerateSelfSignedCertKeyWithOptions` hardcoded `rsa.GenerateKey(cryptorand.Reader, 2048)` for both the CA and the serving certificate, so the apiserver's `--cert-dir` certificates (`server/options/serving.go`) and the loopback client certificate (`serving_with_loopback.go`) could not use a post-quantum key even once the rest of the stack could.

This adds a `KeyGenerator` option to `SelfSignedCertKeyOptions`. It defaults to the existing 2048-bit RSA key, so output is unchanged for every current caller.

Two behaviors follow from the key type rather than from configuration:

* `keyEncipherment` is asserted only for RSA keys. ML-DSA and ECDSA sign only, and asserting the usage for them produces a certificate no library will honor. This implements the note left in `GenerateSelfSignedCertKeyWithOptions` by #142273.
* A non-RSA key is encoded as PKCS#8; RSA keeps its PKCS#1 encoding so the default output is byte-for-byte what it was.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Part of #141838

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Tests cover RSA, ECDSA P-256, and ML-DSA-65. Each generates, parses back through `keyutil.ParsePrivateKeyPEM`, carries the expected key usages, and the serving certificate verifies against the generated CA, so the ML-DSA path is exercised end-to-end.

Rebased on #142273, which has merged. The note it left in GenerateSelfSignedCertKeyWithOptions about key encipherment is removed here, since the key type is now configurable and the usage follows the key.

/assign @everettraven
/sig api-machinery
/sig auth

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
`SelfSignedCertKeyOptions` in `k8s.io/client-go/util/cert` accepts a `KeyGenerator`, allowing self-signed certificates to be generated with a key algorithm other than RSA. The default remains a 2048-bit RSA key.
```

142395.text: Fixed a regression in 1.38 where resource quantities written by a 1.37 or older apiserver with a decimal exponent outside the int32 range, such as `1e4294967296`, could not be decoded, which failed reads of the whole collection.
142395.markdown: Fixed a regression in 1.38 where resource quantities written by a 1.37 or older apiserver with a decimal exponent outside the int32 range, such as `1e4294967296`, could not be decoded, which failed reads of the whole collection. ([#142395](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142395), [@antcybersec](https://github.com/antcybersec)) [SIG API Machinery]
142395.author: antcybersec
142395.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

#141203 started rejecting a decimal exponent that does not fit the int32 scale. A <=1.37 apiserver accepted those spellings, narrowed the exponent to an int32 and stored the object with the text it was given, so master cannot read them back: `ParseQuantity` fails, and per #141166 the etcd3 store fails an entire LIST on the first object it cannot decode.

Following the recipe in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141166#issuecomment-5817729514:

**What v1.37.1 actually does**, measured against the release branch:

| input | v1.37.1 |
| --- | --- |
| `1e4294967296` | parses, `AsInt64` = `(1, true)`, `String()` = `1e4294967296` |
| `1e4294967297` | parses, `AsInt64` = `(10, true)`, `String()` = `10` |
| `-1e4294967296` | parses, `AsInt64` = `(-1, true)` |
| `1e-4294967296` | parses, `AsInt64` = `(1, true)` |
| `1e8589934592` | parses, `AsInt64` = `(1, true)` |
| `1e9223372036854775807` | parses, narrows to `-1`, `String()` = `100e-3` |
| `1e9223372036854775808` | parse error, on 1.37 and on master |
| `1e2147483648`, `1e-2147483648` | parse, then hang while canonicalizing |

So the stored contract is narrowing, not clamping: `1e4294967296` means **1**. Clamping the exponent to `MaxInt32` would decode those objects as astronomically large values instead of the values they hold.

**The tests** in `quantity_compat_test.go` pin the decode path, the re-encode path and the protobuf round trip for the four spellings that 1.37 both accepted and could write. They pass unchanged on `release-1.37` (v1.37.1) and fail on master with `unable to parse quantity's suffix`, which is the regression.

**The fix** narrows the exponent the way 1.37 did. A scale of `math.MinInt32` stays rejected: negating it overflows int32, and 1.37 hung while canonicalizing such a quantity rather than writing it, so no stored object can carry one. That also keeps those two spellings out of the compatibility set, since a test for them could not pass on 1.37.

`TestInterpretExponentInt32Bounds` and the parse error baseline move back to describing the narrowing.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Part of #141166

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Two things deliberately left out, both wanting your call:

- **Rejecting these on write.** With this change `cpu: 1e4294967296` is accepted again and silently means 1. Rejecting it at admission needs the parser to report that it narrowed, which is the strict entry point below rather than something validation can see today.
- **The opt-in strict mode.** Per your note about not shipping a variant that fixes 1 of N, I did not add one here. `1e2147483648` still hangs, and `Add`/`Sub`/`String` still wrap or blow up at extreme scales, so a "strict" `ParseQuantity` today would still hand callers a quantity that hangs later. Happy to add it in a follow-up once those land, or in this PR if you would rather have it now.

/assign @jpbetz
/sig api-machinery

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed a regression in 1.38 where resource quantities written by a 1.37 or older apiserver with a decimal exponent outside the int32 range, such as `1e4294967296`, could not be decoded, which failed reads of the whole collection.
```

YES. Claude Code was used to measure the v1.37.1 behaviour, draft the tests and the fix, and run the verification described above. I reviewed every line and am responsible for the result.

142410.text: Updated google.golang.org/grpc to v1.84.0 to pick up the fix for CVE-2026-84304.
142410.markdown: Updated google.golang.org/grpc to v1.84.0 to pick up the fix for CVE-2026-84304. ([#142410](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142410), [@dims](https://github.com/dims)) [SIG API Machinery, Architecture, Auth, CLI, Cloud Provider, Cluster Lifecycle, Etcd, Instrumentation, Network, Node, Scheduling and Storage]
142410.author: dims
142410.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind dependency

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Bumps `google.golang.org/grpc` from v1.82.2 to v1.84.0 and removes the pin added in #142036.

v1.82.2 does not contain the fix for CVE-2026-84304 (HTTP/2 DATA frame heap exhaustion, GHSA-vp52-pcj8-j9qc). The fix, grpc/grpc-go#9331, shipped only in v1.83.1 and later, and there is no v1.82.x backport. The kubelet gRPC probe client dials servers that pod authors control, so the client side of this bug is reachable from any pod. v1.84.0 also carries the CVE-2026-84303 fix (xDS, which we do not vendor).

grpc v1.83.0+ requires `cloud.google.com/go/auth`, which adds four modules from the unwanted list to the module graph: `s2a-go`, `enterprise-certificate-proxy`, `gax-go/v2` and `google.golang.org/api`. Only `grpc/credentials/google` imports them and we do not vendor that package, so none of them reaches the build list or `vendor/`. This takes option 1 of #142005 and records them in `status.unwantedReferences` with grpc as the only referencer, next to the existing `protoc-gen-validate` and `vtprotobuf` entries. The upstream removal (grpc/grpc-go#9385) is approved but targets grpc 1.86.

The second commit takes what the pin was holding back: the etcd modules to v3.7.2 (they require grpc v1.83.2), `otelgrpc` to v0.71.0 and `otlptracegrpc` to v1.45.0. `otlptracegrpc` v1.46.0 is not taken because it requires `grpc-gateway/v2` v2.30.0, which stays pinned. MVS also moves otel core to v1.46.0, `proto/otlp` to v1.11.0, `golang.org/x/net` to v0.58.0 and `go-logr/logr` to v1.4.4. Five otel modules no longer require `go-spew` or `gopkg.in/yaml.v3` and leave those status lists.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #141798
xref #142005

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

`hack/lint-dependencies.sh` passes after each commit. The four unwanted modules appear only in `go mod graph` with grpc as the importer and have no directory under `vendor/`. The fix is present in the vendored code: `grep -c compactBacklogLocked vendor/google.golang.org/grpc/internal/transport/transport.go` prints 2.

Correction to #141798: the 2026-09-09 comment there says v1.82.2 has the same fix. It does not; v1.82.2 only has the grpc/grpc-go#9365 and #9346 cherry-picks.

142443.text: Fixed API warnings on ReplicationController updates, which described the previous pod template instead of the new one.
142443.markdown: Fixed API warnings on ReplicationController updates, which described the previous pod template instead of the new one. ([#142443](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142443), [@thc1006](https://github.com/thc1006)) [SIG Apps]
142443.author: thc1006
142443.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig apps

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`rcStrategy.WarningsOnUpdate` passes the templates in the wrong order:

```go
		warnings = pod.GetWarningsForPodTemplate(ctx, field.NewPath("spec", "template"), oldRc.Spec.Template, newRc.Spec.Template)
```

`GetWarningsForPodTemplate` takes `(ctx, fieldPath, podTemplate, oldPodTemplate)`, and the other workload strategies pass the new template first. So the warnings on a ReplicationController update describe the template it had before the update.

Before and after on a kind cluster. The `###` lines come from my script, which also prints commands without their shell quoting. Its exit-code lines and blank lines are removed and the file path is shortened, the rest is as printed:

```
### apiserver v1.38.0-alpha.0.1170+dfd7b93a178387
$ kubectl -n rctest apply -f rc.json
replicationcontroller/rc created
$ kubectl -n rctest patch replicationcontroller rc -p {"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"terminationGracePeriodSeconds":-1}}}}
replicationcontroller/rc patched
$ kubectl -n rctest patch replicationcontroller rc -p {"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"terminationGracePeriodSeconds":30}}}}
Warning: spec.template.spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds: must be >= 0; negative values are invalid and will be treated as 1
replicationcontroller/rc patched
### apiserver v1.38.0-alpha.0.1171+00b5ea25a9b98d
$ kubectl -n rctest apply -f rc.json
replicationcontroller/rc created
$ kubectl -n rctest patch replicationcontroller rc -p {"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"terminationGracePeriodSeconds":-1}}}}
Warning: spec.template.spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds: must be >= 0; negative values are invalid and will be treated as 1
replicationcontroller/rc patched
$ kubectl -n rctest patch replicationcontroller rc -p {"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"terminationGracePeriodSeconds":30}}}}
replicationcontroller/rc patched
```

The new test fails on the base commit in the two cases where the order matters. The swap goes back to #101688.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Found while working on #120671, see the special notes.

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

While I was working on #120671, the new warning for `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0` from #142444 showed up after changing an RC from 0 to 1. With both PRs on a kind cluster, changing an RC from 1 to 0 warns and changing it back does not; with #142444 alone it is the other way round. So this one should go in first.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed API warnings on ReplicationController updates, which described the previous pod template instead of the new one.
```

142457.text: kubelet: gRPC probes fail immediately when the connection is refused instead of retrying until the probe timeout. The failure message for a server that never answers is now "timeout: health rpc did not complete within <timeout>".
142457.markdown: Kubelet: gRPC probes fail immediately when the connection is refused instead of retrying until the probe timeout. The failure message for a server that never answers is now "timeout: health rpc did not complete within <timeout>". ([#142457](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142457), [@dims](https://github.com/dims)) [SIG Node and Testing]
142457.author: dims
142457.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind cleanup

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Moves the gRPC probe from the deprecated `grpc.DialContext` with `WithBlock` to `grpc.NewClient`. The client does no I/O until the health check runs, so the one probe timeout still covers connect and RPC. The target uses the `passthrough` resolver, which hands the address to the probe dialer unresolved, as `DialContext` did by default; `NewClient` would otherwise pick the `dns` resolver. Connection errors now surface from the RPC as `Unavailable` and map to the existing "failed to connect" message.

Behavior change: a refused connection fails the probe at once instead of retrying until `timeoutSeconds`, and a server that never answers reports `timeout: health rpc did not complete within <timeout>` instead of `timeout: failed to connect service`. Probe outcomes do not change.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

N/A

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The unreachable-host test, which asserted the old exact timeout text against port 32, is replaced by a connection-refused test on a closed local port that also checks the probe returns well before its 10s timeout. Precedent: #137955 did the same move for cri-client. The second commit fixes a pre-existing flake in two container lifecycle tests (`exit -1` in busybox) that failed this PR's node e2e run; the comment below has the history.

```release-note
kubelet: gRPC probes fail immediately when the connection is refused instead of retrying until the probe timeout. The failure message for a server that never answers is now "timeout: health rpc did not complete within <timeout>".
```

142527.text: Fixed k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/yaml silently dropping the last line of a YAML stream when it has no trailing newline and its length is an exact multiple of the reader buffer size.
142527.markdown: Fixed k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/yaml silently dropping the last line of a YAML stream when it has no trailing newline and its length is an exact multiple of the reader buffer size. ([#142527](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142527), [@SLoeuillet](https://github.com/SLoeuillet)) [SIG API Machinery]
142527.author: SLoeuillet
142527.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig api-machinery

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`YAMLReader` silently dropped the last line of a stream when that line had no trailing newline and a length that is an exact multiple of the buffer size. In that case `LineReader.Read` returns the line together with `io.EOF` (as `io.Reader` allows), and `YAMLReader.Read` discarded it. `YAMLReader.Read` now keeps a line returned with `io.EOF`, ignoring the bare `"\n"` that `LineReader` appends at a normal EOF; writing that one too would make `Read` never return `io.EOF`.

The added test fails at 4096, 8192 and 16384 bytes without the fix, and passes at 4095 and 4097 either way.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142526

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Real-world trigger: Argo CD strips the trailing newline from plugin output before decoding it, so a Helm chart whose last line was 16384 bytes was applied truncated.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/yaml silently dropping the last line of a YAML stream when it has no trailing newline and its length is an exact multiple of the reader buffer size.
```

142607.text: kube-apiserver and other servers built on k8s.io/apiserver now accept up to 16384 request header values. Without this, Go 1.27's default of 500 rejects impersonated or proxied users with about 500 or more groups with HTTP 431. Releases built with Go 1.26 had no separate header-count limit.
142607.markdown: Kube-apiserver and other servers built on k8s.io/apiserver now accept up to 16384 request header values. Without this, Go 1.27's default of 500 rejects impersonated or proxied users with about 500 or more groups with HTTP 431. Releases built with Go 1.26 had no separate header-count limit. ([#142607](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142607), [@cwedgwood](https://github.com/cwedgwood)) [SIG API Machinery and Auth]
142607.author: cwedgwood
142607.pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/kind regression
/sig api-machinery

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Go 1.27 rejects requests with more than 500 header values by default (`http.Server.MaxHeaderValueCount`, golang/go#79936), independently of `MaxHeaderBytes`. Impersonation and request-header authentication carry one header line per group, so a kube-apiserver built with Go 1.27 returns 431 for users with about 500 groups before authentication runs. Details and a reproduction are in #142606.

This sets `MaxHeaderValueCount` to 16384 for secure serving and deprecated insecure serving: the existing 1 MiB `MaxHeaderBytes` at about 64 bytes per value (~16 for the header name and ~48 for the value). The limit stays bounded against floods of tiny headers while accepting identities with thousands of groups.

The new test (Go 1.27 only) serves through `SecureServingInfo` and checks that 1,000 and 16,334 repeated `Impersonate-Group` values reach the handler over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, and that 16,385 are rejected with 431.

With kube-apiserver built from this branch, impersonation and request-header requests with up to 1,000 groups return 200 over both protocols. v1.38.0-alpha.1 returns 431 from 495 groups over HTTP/2 and from 500 over HTTP/1.1.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142606

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

- A constant keeps this change small. Alternatives: a `SecureServingInfo` field so embedders can choose, a flag (an operator knob with no current tuning guidance), or deriving it from `MaxHeaderBytes`.
- Aggregated API servers built on `k8s.io/apiserver` pick this up. Servers that construct their own `http.Server` need the same change.
- `MaxHeaderValueCount` is new in Go 1.27, so `setMaxHeaderValueCount` has a go1.27 build-tagged implementation and a no-op for older Go. This commit applies cleanly to release-1.34 through 1.37 and passes `go vet` there with Go 1.26.8; release-1.34 needs the year-bearing copyright header in the new files.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
kube-apiserver and other servers built on k8s.io/apiserver now accept up to 16384 request header values. Without this, Go 1.27's default of 500 rejects impersonated or proxied users with about 500 or more groups with HTTP 431. Releases built with Go 1.26 had no separate header-count limit.
```

Optionally add one or more of the following kinds if applicable:

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

To route `foo.com/a` to service `svc` on named port `http`, use  `--rule='foo.com/a=svc:http'` 

If a user enters an invalid rule such as:

```
kubectl create ingress demo --rule='foo.com/a=b=svc:http'
```

the command incorrectly accepts it. Instead of returning a clear validation error, `kubectl` later prints a Go array-out-of-bounds stack trace.

```
panic: runtime error: index out of range [1] with length 1
```

During Ingress construction, the rule is split on `=` into:

```
["a", "b", "svc:http"]
```

The code expects the second element to contain complete service configuration in `service-name:port` format, but it gets `b`. It then attempts to parse a service port from `b`. Since `b` contains no `:`, splitting it produces only one element, while code still accesses second element for port. This causes an array-out-of-bounds panic in local `kubectl` process.

Expected behavior: any `--rule` whose path contains an extra `=` or `,` must be rejected as invalid input before Ingress construction begins.

Optionally add one or more of the following kinds if applicable:
/kind api-change

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
`applyconfiguration-gen` looks up root types in the OpenAPI schema by a name derived from their Go package path, while `openapi-gen` names them after the package's `+k8s:openapi-model-package`. When the two differ, the type silently drops out of the generated schema, and its `Extract` functions reference a name the parser doesn't know.

This uses the tag when it is set and otherwise keeps the name derived from the Go package path. It also fails if the schema has no definition for a root type.
